title: Why the Bank of England raised rates before wage pressure was conclusive
summary: The Bank raised Bank Rate to 4% because it judged that waiting for clear evidence of a wage and price response to the energy shock had become costly. All nine members voted for tighter policy. Eight wanted 25 basis points and one wanted 50. At the previous meeting, in September, the Committee had held at 3.75% despite upside inflation risks. What changed was the combination of a further rise in energy prices, a larger stock of costs still to reach customers, and an economy absorbing those costs better than the Bank had expected. For a sterling rates investor, the decision leaves two questions open. How readily will firms and workers start treating higher inflation as a reason to reset prices and pay? And how much restraint has already arrived through higher market borrowing rates before households refinance? The answers can justify tightening now and a lower path several years ahead. The Bank supplied no trade recommendation. (Monetary Policy Summary and Overview, pp. 4–7; Annex 2, p. 89.)

September CPI inflation was 3.5%, up from 2.6% in June and 0.4 percentage points above the July projection. Household energy and motor fuel accounted for around 60% of the excess over the 2% target in September. That denominator matters: it measures the overshoot relative to target, rather than the share of the whole CPI basket or of the increase since June. Much of the forecast error came from motor fuel becoming more expensive when the Bank had expected it to ease. Officials saw a physical supply problem as well as a move in crude futures. Refining constraints kept the margins between refined products and crude unusually wide for diesel and jet fuel. The UK gas futures curve used for the forecast was, on average, about 65% higher than in July. Even if subsequent spot prices followed the declining futures curves assumed in the central projection, changes in regulated household tariffs would still feed through with a lag. Staff projected CPI inflation of 4.9% in 2027 Q2. September is an observation; the following June quarter is a conditional projection. (Section 1.1, Charts 1.1–1.6, pp. 8–15.)

The strongest evidence against an entrenched inflation process came from the behaviour of firms. Existing fixed-price energy contracts and hedges had delayed the shock to bills. Some firms whose costs had risen were accepting lower margins. The first response insulates the income statement for the remaining contract term; the second reduces the resources available to absorb another increase. Both can generate a muted price response today and a larger one later. Staff expected indirect energy effects to add around half a percentage point to CPI inflation in 2027 Q1. That estimate was smaller than in July for the same quarter, yet their estimate for the following quarter was larger. Food illustrates the distinction. The lag between energy or fertiliser purchases and retail food sales gives producers time to adjust. Weather and international agricultural prices could move the retail outcome in addition to the domestic energy shock. Staff saw food inflation potentially reaching around 4¾% in mid-2027. (Section 1.1, Chart 1.3; Box B, pp. 41–46.)

A second-round effect requires a further change in behaviour. If firms reset prices more often, households come to expect higher inflation and workers seek compensation, an initial increase in a few relative prices can spread even as the direct energy contribution fades. Box A finds grounds for vigilance alongside evidence of restraint. Firms with high energy intensity expected faster growth in their own prices. Those expectations are plotted twelve months forward in Chart A.1; treating the diamonds as realised sales prices would exaggerate the evidence. The report’s comparison of sensitive consumer prices pointed to a slower response than during 2022–23. Its dashboard combined elevated household attentiveness with stable survey evidence on the coincidence of firms’ wage and price expectations. Private-sector regular average weekly earnings grew by around 3% in August, while the Decision Maker Panel and Indeed Wage Tracker suggested around 4% pay growth. A shift in employment towards lower-paid industries explains part of that gap. A threshold estimated from historical oil shocks cannot, on its own, establish that UK wage bargaining has moved into a different regime. (Chart 1.7; Box A, Charts A.1–A.3 and Table A.1, pp. 31–40.)

The change in the growth outlook also mattered. Business-to-business services supplied about 0.6 percentage points of the 0.7% growth in GDP in the three months to August against the preceding three months. An industry-based estimate adjusted for trend attributed just under one fifth of GDP growth since the start of 2026 to new AI-related activity. That proxy includes other software and information services. It gives stronger grounds for concluding that investment and demand were being supported than for assuming that broad adoption had already raised potential output. Revised estimates of hours worked also complicate the interpretation of output per hour. Stronger demand at unchanged capacity increases pricing power; stronger productive capacity can accommodate activity with less inflation. On the household side, some spending had held up because households saved less or ran down accumulated savings. Such spending can survive an initial fall in real income without being sustainable through a prolonged one. The Bank still judged there was spare capacity, though several measures suggested it had stopped widening. (Section 1.2; Boxes C and D, pp. 47–58.)

Market rates had already transmitted part of the tightening. The UK forward overnight index swap curve averaged roughly 60 basis points above its July counterpart over the next three years. The November curve used a 15-working-day average ending on 27 October. It reached about 4.9% at end-2027 and about 4.7% in late 2029. By contrast, the median participant in the Bank’s November survey expected 4% in November, 4.25% in February and 3.5% at both the two- and three-year horizons. The Bank interpreted the gap as evidence that risk premia contributed to the upward slope. The survey is a median across respondents. Subtracting it from a forward quote does not give an exact decomposition or an executable excess return. Nor can a curve fixed before the announcement measure the market response to the 5 November publication. (Section 1.3, Chart 1.15, pp. 26–28.)

New two-year fixed mortgage quotes at 75% and 90% loan-to-value had risen around 60 basis points on average since July. The effective rate on the outstanding stock would adjust much more slowly as borrowers refinanced. By end-2029, projected average annual mortgage payments were about £700 above the July projection and £1,500 above the pre-conflict comparison. These are different baselines for the same outcome. New corporate bank lending rates had been broadly flat since July; corporate bond yields had risen, largely with risk-free rates. Real net lending over the year to September remained stronger than a year earlier even as the credit survey signalled softer demand from households and smaller firms in Q3. Volume, price and refinancing-date evidence therefore tell different parts of the transmission story. Box E also finds considerable uncertainty about lags. A brief unexpected rate move in a historical study need not have the same effect as a sustained change in the expected path. (Chart 1.16, pp. 28–30; Box E, pp. 59–64.)

The fiscal assumptions affect the timing of the CPI profile and the later drag on demand. Measures in Budget 2026 were expected to subtract around a quarter of a percentage point from year-on-year CPI inflation in 2027 Q2. As the comparison rolled out a year later, the effect was expected to add around a quarter point in 2028 Q2. That reversal can occur without renewed private-sector price pressure. The Bank expected the new measures to have a limited incremental effect on demand over the forecast, while the planned fiscal consolidation as a whole would increasingly restrain activity. Its longer-run assessment of tax changes also assumed a somewhat larger multiplier with effects that took longer to build. (Box F, pp. 65–68.)

The cleanest way to read the scenarios is to hold the interest rate assumption fixed. All three initially use the same market curve. Under the central projection, four-quarter CPI inflation in 2027 Q4 is 4.0%, up from 2.1% in the July forecast for that quarter. It reaches 2.0% in 2028 Q4 and 1.8% a year later. In the adverse scenario, a higher, more persistent energy path combines with stronger second-round effects. Inflation is 5.5% in 2027 Q4 and 3.0% in 2028 Q4. In the weaker-demand scenario, energy follows the central path, but households and firms have less capacity to absorb costs and spare capacity prevents second-round effects. The corresponding inflation rates are 3.6% and 1.2%. These are conditional outcomes with no probabilities attached. The weaker-demand comparison isolates an important asymmetry for investors: the same energy curve can accompany a materially different medium-term inflation outcome. (Tables 3.A and 3.B; Charts 3.1–3.4; Annex 1.)

Changing the policy assumption asks a different question. One illustrative rule responds to the output gap and non-energy inflation. A second weighs deviations of headline inflation and activity alongside the cost of changing rates. In the baseline, both suggest a broadly similar near-term stance to market pricing but less restraint further out when considered together. In the adverse case, the model-based path averages 0.7 percentage points above its own central path over the forecast; the non-energy rule averages 0.3 points above its equivalent. These comparisons are across scenarios within each rule, not estimates of how far rates must rise from 4%. The models inform the Committee’s discussion and leave room for members to disagree. The practical issue is whether the high near-term inflation peak changes the evidence on future pay and pricing, and whether that evidence arrives before restrictive credit conditions undermine demand. (Section 3.3, Charts 3.5–3.7, pp. 81–84.)

questions.question: Which observations would distinguish deferred cost pass-through from a change in wage and price setting?
questions.detail: A renewed rise in firms’ selling prices could reflect energy contracts rolling over, or an attempt to restore margins and protect expected real wages. Those mechanisms imply different persistence after wholesale prices retreat. Match the timing of contract expiries to later Decision Maker Panel readings on margins, realised prices and wage growth. Then compare energy-intensive firms with firms facing similar demand but lower energy costs. The Bank’s Agents’ pay-settlement evidence and ONS services components would help test whether the repricing spread beyond the firms directly exposed.

questions.question: How much of the upward forward curve represents a higher expected policy path, and how much is compensation for risk?
questions.detail: Chart 1.15 and the survey establish a divergence, but the Bank supplies no precise term-premium estimate or announcement-window position data. For a sterling duration decision, those are different exposures: a reassessment of future votes and a change in the premium can unwind for different reasons. Start with the report’s cited work on risk premia, the distribution of individual Market Participants Survey responses and OIS quotes aligned to the survey dates. A comparison across tenors and forecast vintages would be more informative than a single median-minus-forward calculation.

questions.question: Which households will encounter both a mortgage reset and an exhausted saving buffer?
questions.detail: Aggregate spending and net lending had held up while new borrowing costs rose. The report quantifies the eventual average mortgage-payment increase but does not establish which refinancing cohorts also have few liquid assets. A concentrated income squeeze could lead the aggregate indicators. Compare the Bank’s mortgage-reset profiles and NMG household survey by fixed-rate expiry, liquid savings and income. Track whether spending falls first in exposed cohorts or declines broadly, which would change the weight placed on the weaker-demand scenario.

questions.question: Could stronger business investment add productive capacity fast enough to change the projected output gap?
questions.detail: The report identifies strength in technology-related services and investment and acknowledges uncertainty about hours worked. It cannot yet establish how much of the measured output is installation activity, or how quickly downstream businesses will use it to produce more per hour. Use ONS industry-level investment, revised hours and output data alongside the Bank’s Agents’ evidence on adoption and utilisation. Sustained gains in adopting sectors would support a different interpretation of resilient growth from a spending surge confined to suppliers.
